title: A wallet's profit engine isn't interest on balances, it's money moving inside the system
dek: The core ledger of a wallet: money coming in pays card-network tolls, internal transfers cost almost nothing, and money going out can be charged again. It earns the spread on flow, not interest on deposits — PayPal, Cash App and Stripe Link are all betting on this model.
why: It takes the wallet cost structure apart for real: wholesale network pricing under ten cents, while platforms can charge users several times that; Japanese players even open accounts at multiple banks to route around clearing. Useful as a business teardown even if you don't do payments.
who: Product and strategy people in payments, wallets and acquiring, especially anyone trying to understand how PayPal, Stripe and Cash App compete.
skip: 14:49 to 18:09 is a Mercury and Granola sponsor read; skip straight past it.

points.h: A wallet has to answer on day one how it makes money
points.body: It opens with the author's own $100 Venmo bill to a barber: for a small transaction that already has a mature payment rail, why does PayPal still want to wedge itself in and monetize it. Then it quickly sets the scope: this is about the e-wallet business, not crypto private-key wallets; because it looks like it can hold and disburse balances, it immediately enters the regulatory zone that treats deposits as sensitive, so a wallet has to answer from the first day of design how it makes money — fail that, and the product dies.

points.h: Card fraud isn't scammers building sites, it's leakage at the issuer
points.body: The biggest early obstacle to online transactions was that users didn't dare hand over their card numbers, and the media kept amplifying card-fraud risk. The author points out the facts are the opposite: most fraud comes from massive data breaches at the issuer end, not from fraudsters parasitizing checkout sites, and concludes that "economies of scale protect criminals too." PayPal's value was standing between the user and the card number and the recipient, capping the risk of a single transaction — which gave it grounds to charge a toll near 3%, and planted the seed for the balance design that followed.

points.h: A free wallet is not free at all for the wallet itself
points.body: Putting money into a wallet goes through the card networks, at a historical list price of about 3%, and that cost is borne by the wallet; but once the balance stays inside the system, transfers between users amount to changing a row in a database, too cheap to bill for. PayPal charges close to full price on both the in and out ends, so simply substituting internal transfers for external ones adds a slice of gross margin. A wallet that is free to the average user is not free to the wallet — the zero marginal cost of the float is the real dam.

points.h: Beating down the network fee makes more money than product innovation
points.body: There is no necessary relationship between wholesale and retail: buying millions of ACH transactions costs about $0.05 each, while a payment provider can quote merchants close to $0.30; the spread is the tax the platform levies on the underlying plumbing. Japan is more extreme: interbank transfers cost about ¥200 per transaction, while an intra-bank entry is nearly free, so some products open accounts at each of the top banks, let users' money move inside the banks, and settle via daily netting. In finance, beating down the network fee converts into wallet profit more directly than product innovation.

points.h: Cash-out isn't a user perk, it's a second toll pipe
points.body: Cash App prices cash-out the same way: want it fast, pick the pricier card rail, charged at 1.75% with a 25-cent minimum; the author tested withdrawing $50 and was quoted 88 cents. Paired with that is issuing prepaid cards through partners like Sutton Bank, so money spent outside the system still captures swipe fees. The wallet no longer treats cash-out as a user perk but as a second revenue pipe, because the partner bank needs the wallet's user scale and the wallet needs the bank's issuing license.

points.h: On co-brand cards the wallet takes a cut and carries the bad debt
points.body: The logic of a wallet co-branding a credit card is charging on both sides, but risk control is the real battlefield: wallets usually assume the spending data they've accumulated lets them underwrite more accurately than the issuing bank. The industry has repeatedly shown FICO is already strong enough to be hard to replace; the extra variables that could materially improve losses often cross legal red lines. What actually prices the wallet is the agreement — the bank requires the whole loan portfolio's loss rate to stay under a threshold, or the wallet's revenue share goes to zero or even turns negative. The 10-K language dances around "loss sharing," but in essence the wallet is carrying the issuer's bad debt.

points.h: Users care about the phone, not the plastic card
points.body: Apple's core argument when negotiating with banks is that users care about the phone, not the plastic credit card; if banks won't pay, Apple can also back or build a new two-sided payment network and take users with it. The reported figure is that Apple takes 15 basis points per Apple Pay transaction, while Google reportedly takes nothing — the author uses this to gripe about the two giants' differing ability to do non-core products. The next layer is the conclusion that the checkout itself can be an ad slot: once the goods and price are fixed, who gets to rank a payment method first becomes a bidding position, and Stripe has already turned the traditional display into dynamic ordering by user preference, even opening up merchant fine-tuning options.

points.h: Network fees don't fall at the negotiating table, they fall in the default setting
points.body: Extend Link into a general-ledger-level settlement negotiating layer: if users store their low-cost payment methods in Link, the next checkout can bypass the card networks and go through a bank account; the network fee saved is then redistributed between merchant and user. This can't be negotiated by one company sitting at one table — it's the aggregation of millions of users' and merchants' decisions, ultimately making the side it represents at the payments negotiating table approach 1% of global GDP. Only that kind of volume earns the right to reprice the network fee.

terms.def: The US interbank batch transfer network; direct debits and credits are extremely cheap, with wholesale pricing as low as $0.05 per transaction.
The portion of a card transaction's rate that goes to the issuing bank, usually a percentage of transaction value; the wallet model's goal is to bypass it.
A small US bank exempt from the debit-card interchange cap under US regulation, often the actual issuer behind a wallet's co-brand card.
A unit of financial pricing; 1 basis point equals 0.01%, so 15 bps is 0.15%.
